title: Migrating 7-Year Legacy ERP to Medallion Data Warehouse with CDC & Zero Data Loss
summary: Extracting MySQL binlogs via Change Data Capture, implementing idempotent Go workers on RabbitMQ, and cutting analytics query latency by 70% with zero downtime.
author: Huỳnh Nhật Tân

sections.business-data-requirements: An ERP system running for 7 years accumulated massive retail transactions. The Business Intelligence (BI) and executive teams required hourly near-real-time reports. However, the legacy OLTP MySQL database with bloated Entity-Attribute-Value (EAV) tables suffered 100% CPU spikes during heavy reporting queries.
sections.data-modeling:
We decoupled OLAP from OLTP by implementing a Medallion Architecture (Data Lakehouse) on PostgreSQL/ClickHouse:

  • Bronze Tier (Raw Ingestion): Append-only tables preserving original JSON event payloads extracted from MySQL binlogs.
  • Silver Tier (Cleaned & Conformed): Normalized Third Normal Form (3NF) models with sanitized types and foreign key relationships.
  • Gold Tier (Dimensional Star Schema): Fact tables for sales/inventory and Dimension tables for customers and products optimized for BI tools.
sections.pipeline-construction:
The CDC pipeline operated non-intrusively without touching legacy ERP application code:

  • Binary Log Ingestion (CDC): Debezium/Canal listening to MySQL row-based binlogs and dispatching events to RabbitMQ.
  • Idempotent Go Workers: High-concurrency Golang workers consuming queue messages and executing upserts with ON CONFLICT (id, version) DO UPDATE.
  • Dead Letter Exchange (DLX): Corrupted records or network failures routed to retry queues with exponential backoff.
sections.testing-optimization:
Verification and performance tuning included:

  • Data Reconciliation: Automated nightly checksum and row count validation between MySQL OLTP and PostgreSQL Warehouse.
  • Tuning: Monthly table partitioning, BRIN indexes on query timestamps, and micro-batching writes at 500 records per transaction.
  • End-to-End Latency: Transaction commit to warehouse availability reduced to under 1.8 seconds.
sections.summary-recommendations: Achieved 96% data reconciliation accuracy with 0% data loss and slashed analytics query execution time by 70%. Recommendation: Always enforce Idempotency Keys and Schema Registries from day one.

title: High-Throughput Event Ingestion Architecture with Spring WebFlux, Kafka & Automated PII Anonymization
summary: Building a privacy-compliant MarTech ingestion gateway handling tens of thousands of real-time e-commerce events per second with sub-second latency.
author: Huỳnh Nhật Tân

sections.context-problem: During peak e-commerce promotional events, user traffic surges 15-20x. The tracking gateway must ingest tens of thousands of micro-events/sec (cart adds, product views, checkout clicks) for real-time dispatch to Google Analytics 4 and Facebook Conversions API without degrading user browsing performance.
sections.system-requirements:
• Functional: Real-time ingestion, validation, categorization, and dispatch to downstream ad-tech platforms.
  • Non-Functional: p99 API latency < 15ms, throughput capacity of 10,000 RPS, automated PII sanitization, and zero data loss on third-party outages.
sections.architecture-design:
Designed as a non-blocking Reactive Event-Driven pipeline:

  • Ingestion Layer: Spring WebFlux (Project Reactor + Netty) receiving asynchronous HTTP requests and streaming directly to Apache Kafka clusters.
  • Privacy & Sanitization: Spring AOP and custom Jackson serializers recursively detecting sensitive fields (emails, phones, IDs) and applying Salted SHA-256 hashing before outbound dispatch.
  • Outbox & Delivery: Kafka worker services consuming events and communicating with external APIs via non-blocking WebClient.
sections.trade-offs-analysis:
Comparing Synchronous vs Reactive architectures:

  • Synchronous (Spring MVC + Tomcat): Straightforward debugging, but thread-per-request model leads to thread exhaustion under 5,000 concurrent connections.
  • Reactive Non-Blocking (Spring WebFlux): Steeper learning curve for stream operations and backpressure management, but sustains 20,000+ RPS stably on minimal CPU cores with 60% lower RAM utilization.
sections.lessons-best-practices: Integrate Resilience4j Circuit Breakers and exponential backoff retries at the outbound gateway layer. Never perform blocking I/O operations on WebFlux event loop threads.

title: Optimizing Multi-Stage Docker (<25MB) & Building Zero-Downtime CI/CD Pipeline with GitHub Actions
summary: Lightweight Alpine packaging strategies, Nginx SPA fallback configurations, and automated static typechecks in continuous release pipelines.
author: Huỳnh Nhật Tân

sections.article-objectives: Guide to building ultra-lightweight SPA web container images (< 25MB) using Docker Multi-Stage Builds on Alpine Linux, coupled with automated GitHub Actions CI/CD for Zero-Downtime Deployments.
sections.architecture-principles:
Two distinct deployment stages:

  • Stage 1 (Builder): node:20-alpine image installs dependencies, executes linting/typechecking, and produces optimized static assets in /dist.
  • Stage 2 (Production Runner): Only the compiled /dist folder is copied into nginx:alpine-slim (< 15MB) with gzip compression and secure HTTP headers.
  • GitHub Actions Pipeline: Automatically triggered on PR/Push to main: Lint -> Test -> Build -> Docker Push -> Deploy.
sections.step-by-step-setup:
Configuration details:

  • Step 1: Multi-stage Dockerfile with non-root user and .dockerignore excluding node_modules and extraneous docs.
  • Step 2: nginx.conf configured with try_files $uri $uri/ /index.html; and static cache headers.
  • Step 3: Workflow .github/workflows/deploy.yml leveraging Docker Buildx cache to speed up CI runs by 3x.
sections.troubleshooting-pitfalls:
• 404 on page refresh in SPA: Missing Nginx fallback to index.html. Resolved with try_files directive.
  • Bloated images: Caused by copying devDependencies into the final image without multi-stage builds.
  • Security risks: Running containers as root. Fixed by specifying USER nginx.
sections.evaluation-scaling: Reduced Docker image size from 850MB to 22MB and deployment time from 6 minutes to under 45 seconds. Future roadmap: Integrate Trivy container vulnerability scanning and Kubernetes canary rollouts.

title: Building High-Performance Concurrent Worker Pool in Golang with Context & Graceful Shutdown
summary: Bounded concurrent job queue pattern using fixed goroutines, context.Context timeout control, and graceful OS signal handling.
author: Huỳnh Nhật Tân

sections.problem-statement: When processing millions of database I/O records or dispatching batch email notifications, spawning an unbounded goroutine per task (go processTask(t)) rapidly causes out-of-memory crashes and database connection pool exhaustion.
sections.initial-approach: Initial naive implementations often rely on sync.WaitGroup across unbounded goroutines. Under a spike of 50,000 tasks, the server consumes multiple Gigabytes of memory and the database rejects connection requests.
sections.optimization-thinking:
Designed a Bounded Concurrency Worker Pool:

  • Buffered channels act as task queues to prevent memory bloat.
  • Fixed N worker goroutines continuously listen on the task channel.
  • context.WithCancel or context.WithTimeout enables graceful task abortion on long-running timeouts.
sections.code-implementation:
Implemented a WorkerPool struct managing channels and graceful shutdown:

type WorkerPool struct {
  workers int
  tasks   chan Task
  wg      sync.WaitGroup
  ctx     context.Context
  cancel  context.CancelFunc
}

Upon receiving SIGTERM, the pool closes the task channel and waits for active workers to finish pending work before exiting.
sections.complexity-applications: Maintains fixed O(N) memory complexity relative to worker count, sustaining 8,000 tasks/sec throughput under 50MB RAM. Widely applicable in data ingestion, batch ETL, and webhook dispatch engines.

title: Tech Radar 2026: Pragmatic Evaluation of Adopting Rust in Enterprise Backend Systems
summary: Multi-dimensional analysis on memory safety, CPU throughput, developer learning curve, and lessons learned from deploying Rust in production microservices.
author: Huỳnh Nhật Tân

sections.introduction: In the 2026 technology landscape, Rust has emerged as a premier language for critical infrastructure. This article shares practical engineering insights from prototyping and shipping a high-throughput microservice in Rust (Actix-web / Tokio) in enterprise production.
sections.multi-dimensional-evaluation:
Comprehensive evaluation across core criteria:

  • Strengths: Memory safety without Garbage Collection overhead, remarkably low memory footprint (< 15MB for active web instances), and nearly zero runtime bugs due to the expressive type system and borrow checker.
  • Challenges: Longer compilation times, higher hiring and training costs, and fewer turnkey enterprise ORM integrations compared to mature Java or Go ecosystems.
sections.case-study-experience: Rewrote a high-volume JWT token verification and rate-limiting gateway from Node.js to Rust. Outcome: p99 latency dropped from 18ms to 1.2ms, CPU utilization reduced by 75%, and GC latency jitter was completely eliminated.
sections.actionable-recommendations: Recommendation: Avoid wholesale rewrites. Begin adoption on performance-sensitive edge proxies, cryptographic engines, or CPU-intensive data pipelines before expanding to team-wide initiatives.
sections.open-questions-discussion: Will the rise of Java Virtual Threads and Go concurrency diminish the performance advantage of Rust for standard CRUD web backends? We invite your thoughts.

title: Scaling ERP Reporting Portal for 1,000+ Concurrent Users with Redis & Node.js
summary: Heavy reporting query caching techniques, asynchronous batch processing, and modular interface design strategies.
author: Huỳnh Nhật Tân

sections.context-problem: During end-of-month financial closing periods, over 1,000 enterprise clients simultaneously requested ledger balance and inventory reports. The relational database suffered severe I/O bottlenecks, causing API response times to exceed 12 seconds.
sections.system-requirements:
• Throughput & Latency: Serve 1,000+ concurrent enterprise users while keeping 95th percentile API response times under 800ms.
  • Data Freshness: Financial reports must reflect ledger changes within 5 minutes.
sections.architecture-design:
Layered caching and asynchronous worker architecture:

  • Multi-Level Caching: Redis Cluster storing serialized JSON aggregates with 5-minute TTLs and proactive cache warm-up cron jobs.
  • Asynchronous Export Queue: Large Excel/PDF reporting jobs offloaded to background BullMQ workers, delivering download URLs via WebSocket on completion.
sections.trade-offs-analysis:
Balancing Immediate Consistency vs High Availability:

  • Accepted a 5-minute data staleness window on cached reporting views in exchange for an 85% reduction in direct database query load.
  • Implemented event-driven cache invalidation when high-priority ledger settlements occurred.
sections.lessons-best-practices: Implement distributed Mutex Locks (Redlock) to prevent Cache Stampedes and Cache Avalanches when hot cache keys expire under heavy traffic spikes.

title: Building Real-time Financial Ledger Aggregation Pipeline with ClickHouse for Millions of Transactions
summary: Leveraging ClickHouse columnar storage and SummingMergeTree engines to calculate ledger reconciliation balances in under 50ms.
author: Huỳnh Nhật Tân

sections.business-data-requirements: The financial department required instantaneous balance sheet analysis across 50+ million monthly retail transactions. PostgreSQL GROUP BY and SUM queries took over 25 seconds per chart refresh.
sections.data-modeling:
Optimized table schema in ClickHouse:

  • SummingMergeTree Engine: Automatically aggregates debit/credit amounts during background merge passes, eliminating 90% of row scans during query time.
  • Partitioning: Monthly partitioning with toYYYYMM(transaction_date) and primary key ordering by (account_id, currency, transaction_date).
sections.pipeline-construction:
Streaming pipeline architecture:

  • Real-time event streaming from Kafka via ClickHouse Kafka Engine tables.
  • Direct ingestion and data transformation via Materialized Views without requiring intermediate worker application layers.
sections.testing-optimization: Performance benchmarks across 100 million ledger rows: Query execution dropped from 28 seconds to 38ms. Achieved a 6.5x data compression ratio over raw SSD disk usage.
sections.summary-recommendations: ClickHouse is exceptionally suited for high-volume financial analytics. Recommendation: Avoid single-row inserts; always batch writes between 10,000 and 100,000 records.

title: Zero-Downtime Blue-Green Deployments with Docker Compose & Nginx Reverse Proxy
summary: Production release architecture using alternating environments and automated Nginx upstream switching via shell scripts.
author: Huỳnh Nhật Tân

sections.article-objectives: Implement zero-downtime release automation for medium-scale enterprise web services using Blue-Green deployments with instant rollback safety.
sections.architecture-principles:
Two identical containerized environments:

  • Blue (Live): Actively serving production traffic on port 8081.
  • Green (Idle): Receives new version releases on port 8082, executes migrations, and validates smoke tests.
  • Nginx Proxy: Routes traffic and issues nginx -s reload for seamless upstream switching.
sections.step-by-step-setup:
Deployment pipeline stages:

  • Step 1: Pull updated Docker image and spin up the idle environment (Green).
  • Step 2: Execute health check validation on /healthz until HTTP 200 is verified.
  • Step 3: Atomically update Nginx upstream configuration and execute reload.
  • Step 4: Gracefully stop the previous environment after a 60-second in-flight draining window.
sections.troubleshooting-pitfalls:
• Database Schema Incompatibility: Occurs when migrations remove columns still read by the old version. Solve via the Expand and Contract pattern.
  • Dropped TCP Connections: Ensure Nginx is reloaded with HUP signal so old worker processes finish existing requests before terminating.
sections.evaluation-scaling: Eliminated midnight maintenance windows, allowing continuous deployments 5-10 times daily with confidence and zero user disruption.

title: Deep Dive: Java 21 Virtual Threads (Project Loom) vs Reactive Streams in Microservices
summary: Comprehensive architectural comparison of Thread-per-Request concurrency with Virtual Threads against Reactive Programming (Project Reactor/RxJava) across performance, syntax clarity, and observability.
author: Huỳnh Nhật Tân

sections.problem-statement: Prior to Java 21, handling tens of thousands of concurrent connections with blocking I/O required rewriting code to Reactive Streams (Spring WebFlux, RxJava). However, reactive pipelines introduce steep cognitive complexity, fragmented stack traces, and fragile ThreadLocal contexts.
sections.initial-approach: Standard Platform Threads (1 Java Thread = 1 OS Thread) hit hard limits around 2,000 - 3,000 threads due to 1MB stack memory allocations and costly OS context switching overhead.
sections.optimization-thinking:
Java 21 Virtual Threads (Project Loom) introduces lightweight user-mode threads scheduled by the JVM:

  • Millions of Virtual Threads run on a small pool of Carrier OS threads.
  • Upon encountering blocking I/O (JDBC queries, outbound REST calls), the JVM automatically unmounts the virtual thread without blocking the underlying carrier thread.
  • Enables writing straightforward, sequential code with crystal-clear stack traces.
sections.code-implementation:
Enabling Virtual Threads in Spring Boot 3.2+ is as simple as configuring spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true or utilizing ExecutorService:

try (var executor = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
  IntStream.range(0, 100_000).forEach(i -> executor.submit(() -> {
    fetchRemoteApi(i);
  }));
}
sections.complexity-applications: Delivers 90-95% of Reactive Streams throughput with 50% lower maintenance overhead. Ideal for I/O-bound microservices, enterprise CRUD APIs, and payment orchestrators.

title: Tech Lead Insights: Balancing Technical Debt and Feature Delivery Velocity
summary: A pragmatic engineering governance framework to maintain codebase health, prevent operational outages, and sustain business feature delivery commitments.
author: Huỳnh Nhật Tân

sections.introduction: One of the primary challenges for a Technical Team Lead is balancing commercial pressure for rapid feature delivery against the vital need to address technical debt and preserve system stability.
sections.multi-dimensional-evaluation:
Categorizing technical debt into 3 distinct quadrants:

  • Deliberate Debt: Consciously taking shortcuts to validate market hypotheses with a committed refactoring plan within 1 sprint.
  • Architectural Decay: Legacy systems outgrown by current scale requirements.
  • Accidental Debt: Incurred via rushed code reviews, missing automated tests, or junior knowledge gaps.
sections.case-study-experience: Adopted The 20% Sprint Budget Rule: Allocating a fixed 20% of story points in every sprint toward architectural refactoring, security upgrades, and test automation. Outcome: Production defect rates dropped by 60% across 3 quarters.
sections.actionable-recommendations: Quantify technical debt in financial and business terms (e.g. estimated outage costs, engineer hours lost per sprint) when aligning priorities with Product Managers and Executives.
sections.open-questions-discussion: How does your organization prioritize technical debt alongside feature roadmaps? What strategies have worked best for your team?

title: Designing Absolute Idempotent Payment & Webhook Processing in Distributed Systems
summary: Protecting financial transactions against duplicate webhook deliveries using Distributed Locks, Idempotency Keys, and Transactional Outbox patterns.
author: Huỳnh Nhật Tân

sections.context-problem: Payment gateways (Stripe, VNPay, MoMo) frequently retry webhooks upon transient network timeouts. Without robust idempotency handling, user wallets risk double-crediting or duplicate order fulfillment.
sections.system-requirements:
• Financial Correctness: Zero tolerance for double-spending or duplicate order processing.
  • Performance: Sub-300ms webhook acknowledgment response times to external providers.
sections.architecture-design:
Multi-layered defensive architecture:

  • Tier 1 (Idempotency Key Store): PostgreSQL table enforcing unique constraints on PRIMARY KEY (provider_name, idempotency_key).
  • Tier 2 (Distributed Redis Lock): Temporary mutex locking with SET lock_key token NX PX 5000 during active transaction execution.
  • Tier 3 (Strict State Machine): Enforcing unidirectional state transitions (e.g. PENDING -> PAID, rejecting duplicate PAID transitions).
sections.trade-offs-analysis:
Pessimistic vs Optimistic concurrency control:

  • Optimistic locking with version counters handles general order updates efficiently.
  • Pessimistic Redis distributed locks are applied to critical financial balance debits to guarantee race-free mutations.
sections.lessons-best-practices: Persist raw webhook payloads to audit tables prior to processing, and return immediate HTTP 200 OK responses if a duplicate key has already been settled successfully.

title: Implementing High-Performance Slowly Changing Dimensions (SCD Type 2) in Big Data ETL Pipelines
summary: Tracking historical customer and product attribute mutations over time with dbt, PostgreSQL, and high-performance temporal range indexes.
author: Huỳnh Nhật Tân

sections.business-data-requirements: When customers update shipping addresses or loyalty tiers (VIP to Diamond), historical revenue reports must reflect the customer's tier at the time of purchase rather than overwriting past transactions.
sections.data-modeling:
SCD Type 2 dimensional modeling schema:

  • surrogate_key: Unique synthetic primary key for each record revision.
  • valid_from & valid_to: Temporal validity boundaries (e.g., 9999-12-31 for active records).
  • is_current: Boolean flag marking active current revisions.
sections.pipeline-construction:
Automated snapshotting with dbt (data build tool):

  • Apply check or timestamp strategies to automatically capture delta mutations.
  • Execute atomic MERGE statements to expire old revisions (UPDATE valid_to = now()) and insert new versions.
sections.testing-optimization: Created GiST (customer_id, daterange(valid_from, valid_to)) exclusion constraints to mathematically prevent overlapping validity windows across versions of the same entity.
sections.summary-recommendations: SCD Type 2 is vital for historical reporting integrity. Recommendation: Apply SCD Type 2 selectively to high-value dimensions (Customers, Products) rather than high-frequency telemetry tables.

title: Configuring Production Kubernetes Ingress & Automated SSL/TLS with Cert-Manager and Let's Encrypt
summary: Step-by-step setup of Ingress-Nginx, automated zero-touch certificate issuance and renewals with Let's Encrypt ACME ClusterIssuers.
author: Huỳnh Nhật Tân

sections.article-objectives: Fully automate SSL/TLS certificate issuance, provisioning, and renewals for production Kubernetes clusters, eliminating the risk of operational downtime from expired certificates.
sections.architecture-principles:
Ingress security architecture:

  • Ingress-Nginx Controller: Edge proxy routing external HTTP/HTTPS traffic to internal Kubernetes Services.
  • Cert-Manager Operator: Kubernetes Custom Controller monitoring Certificate CRDs and solving Let's Encrypt ACME HTTP-01/DNS-01 challenges.
  • Kubernetes Secrets: Storing TLS keypairs (tls.crt, tls.key) mounted into Ingress resources.
sections.step-by-step-setup:
Implementation roadmap:

  • Step 1: Deploy Cert-Manager via official Helm charts with installCRDs=true.
  • Step 2: Configure production ClusterIssuer pointing to Let's Encrypt ACME v2 endpoints.
  • Step 3: Annotate Ingress manifests with cert-manager.io/cluster-issuer: letsencrypt-prod.
sections.troubleshooting-pitfalls:
• HTTP-01 Challenge Failed: Cloud Security Groups blocking inbound port 80 (Let's Encrypt requires port 80 for domain validation).
  • Let's Encrypt Rate Limits: Always validate configurations against Let's Encrypt Staging issuers first.
sections.evaluation-scaling: Automated SSL certificate renewals across 50+ enterprise subdomains 30 days prior to expiration with zero human intervention.

title: Crafting Clean Code: Eliminating God Objects and Refactoring Anemic Domain Models
summary: Strategies for decomposing bloated multi-thousand line classes into cohesive Aggregate Roots adhering to Clean Code and Object-Oriented principles.
author: Huỳnh Nhật Tân

sections.problem-statement: In legacy codebases, service classes like OrderService frequently explode beyond 3,000 lines with dozens of dependencies. Entities degenerate into dumb data bags with public getters/setters (Anemic Domain Model), scattering critical business logic throughout the application.
sections.initial-approach: Developers often append more conditional if/else branches or create static utility classes, worsening coupling and violating the Single Responsibility Principle.
sections.optimization-thinking:
Transition to a Rich Domain Model:

  • Encapsulate domain validations and state transitions directly within Entities.
  • Eliminate public setters and enforce invariant constraints upon entity creation.
  • Employ Domain Events for cross-aggregate communication instead of direct service coupling.
sections.code-implementation:
Refactoring domain logic into encapsulated entities:

public class Order {
  private OrderStatus status;
  private List items;

  public void applyDiscount(DiscountCode code) {
    if (this.status != OrderStatus.DRAFT) {
      throw new IllegalStateException("Cannot discount confirmed order");
    }
    // Encapsulated domain logic
  }
}
sections.complexity-applications: Decreased Cyclomatic Complexity by 60%, boosted unit test coverage beyond 85%, and allowed new engineering team members to comprehend domain rules intuitively.

title: Backend Architecture Evolution: From Monolith to Microservices and the Rise of Modular Monolith
summary: A 10-year retrospective on architectural trends, evaluating the hidden operational costs of microservices and why Modular Monoliths represent the pragmatic choice for modern engineering teams.
author: Huỳnh Nhật Tân

sections.introduction: The rush to adopt Microservices dominated the past decade. By 2026, leading engineering organizations are pragmatically consolidating systems into Modular Monoliths to reduce distributed network friction and cloud operational overhead.
sections.multi-dimensional-evaluation:
Comparative analysis of architectural paradigms:

  • Traditional Monolith: Simple deployment, but risks becoming an unmaintainable Big Ball of Mud without strict code boundaries.
  • Microservices: Autonomous team deployments, yet incurs high network latency, distributed transaction complexity (Sagas), and observability friction.
  • Modular Monolith: Strict Bounded Context boundaries within a single deployable artifact. Leverages ultra-fast in-memory calls with seamless readiness for future microservice extraction.
sections.case-study-experience: Consolidated 6 fragmented microservices into a unified Go Modular Monolith. AWS infrastructure costs dropped 65%, inter-service gRPC timeouts disappeared, and feature development throughput doubled.
sections.actionable-recommendations: Start with a well-bounded Modular Monolith. Only decompose into Microservices when independent hardware scaling or organizational boundaries (>50 engineers) truly necessitate it.
sections.open-questions-discussion: Has your engineering team experienced 'Microservices Fatigue'? What architectural boundaries have worked best in your domain?

title: Applying Domain-Driven Design (DDD) & Hexagonal Architecture in Golang Microservices
summary: Structuring Go services with Ports & Adapters to decouple core domain business rules from external frameworks, SQL drivers, and transport protocols.
author: Huỳnh Nhật Tân

sections.context-problem: In naive Golang projects, SQL queries and HTTP JSON parsing often intermingle inside handlers. Swapping databases or adding gRPC interfaces forces intrusive rewrites across business logic.
sections.system-requirements:
• Technology Independence: Core domain rules must remain free from external libraries and database drivers.
  • Testability: 100% unit test coverage for use cases using mock interfaces without live database connections.
sections.architecture-design:
Ports & Adapters (Hexagonal Architecture) structure:

  • Domain Core: Pure entities and domain services importing standard Go libraries only.
  • Ports: Contracts defined as Go interfaces (e.g. UserRepository, PaymentGateway).
  • Adapters: Concrete implementations (HTTP Handlers, gRPC Servers, PostgreSQL Repositories, Redis Caches).
sections.trade-offs-analysis:
Initial boilerplate vs long-term maintainability:

  • Hexagonal architecture requires additional interface declarations and data transfer mappings up front.
  • In exchange, long-term maintenance costs drop by 50% as underlying database drivers and cloud infrastructure evolve.
sections.lessons-best-practices: Define Port interfaces in the consumer package (Consumer Interface pattern in Go) rather than bundling them alongside the adapter implementations.

title: PostgreSQL Optimization for Multi-Billion Row Tables: Monthly Partitioning & BRIN Indexes
summary: Partitioning strategy for massive audit/event tables and utilizing Block Range Indexes (BRIN) to cut index memory footprint by 95% compared to conventional B-Trees.
author: Huỳnh Nhật Tân

sections.business-data-requirements: User telemetry and GPS tracking systems logged over 2 billion rows annually. When table size exceeded 500GB, traditional B-Tree indexes consumed 120GB of RAM, exceeding database buffer cache and causing severe analytical query degradation.
sections.data-modeling:
Relational partitioning architecture:

  • Declarative Partitioning: Splitting the primary table by monthly time ranges via PARTITION BY RANGE (created_at).
  • Partition Pruning: Allowing the PostgreSQL query planner to completely bypass non-relevant child tables during range filter evaluations.
sections.pipeline-construction:
Implementing Block Range Indexes (BRIN):

  • Because time-series data is written monotonically in ascending physical block order, BRIN only tracks min/max summaries per 128 disk pages (pages_per_range = 128).
  • Automated upcoming month partition creation using the pg_partman extension.
sections.testing-optimization: Performance gains: Total index size plummeted from 120GB to just 450MB (over 99% reduction). Range scan throughput accelerated by 5x due to precise Partition Pruning.
sections.summary-recommendations: BRIN indexes are ideal for append-only time-series datasets in PostgreSQL. Recommendation: Schedule periodic VACUUM ANALYZE maintenance to preserve BRIN block metadata accuracy.

title: End-to-End Distributed Tracing with OpenTelemetry, Prometheus and Grafana for Spring Boot
summary: Tracking distributed request lifecycles across microservice clusters, diagnosing latency bottlenecks, and rendering live Service Dependency Graphs.
author: Huỳnh Nhật Tân

sections.article-objectives: Establish a comprehensive Observability ecosystem for Spring Boot microservices, enabling engineering teams to identify and resolve distributed latency spikes within minutes.
sections.architecture-principles:
Unified three pillars of Observability (Tracing, Metrics, Logs):

  • OpenTelemetry Java Agent: Automatically injects and propagates Trace and Span IDs across asynchronous HTTP calls via W3C Trace Context headers.
  • OpenTelemetry Collector: Ingests telemetry, sanitizes sensitive parameters, and routes data to Prometheus and Grafana Tempo.
  • Grafana Dashboard: Visualizes live Service Dependency Graphs and facilitates seamless jumps from Metric Alerts directly into correlated Traces.
sections.step-by-step-setup:
Configuration details:

  • Step 1: Attach opentelemetry-javaagent.jar inside the production Spring Boot Dockerfile.
  • Step 2: Set environment variable OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT=http://otel-collector:4317.
  • Step 3: Configure Prometheus alert rules utilizing the RED method (Rate, Errors, Duration).
sections.troubleshooting-pitfalls:
• Context Propagation Loss in Async Threads: Occurs when switching threads without wrapping Context.current(). Fixed via custom Spring TaskDecorators.
  • Network Bandwidth Bloat: Configure Tail-based Sampling on Otel Collector to capture 100% of error traces while sampling only 5% of healthy traces.
sections.evaluation-scaling: Decreased Mean Time to Detection (MTTD) and Mean Time to Resolution (MTTR) from 45 minutes down to under 3 minutes across production fleets.

title: Mastering Advanced TypeScript: Discriminated Unions, Type Guards and Generic Constraints in Practice
summary: Leveraging TypeScript's expressive type system to eliminate impossible UI states at compile-time and design rock-solid Type-Safe application interfaces.
author: Huỳnh Nhật Tân

sections.problem-statement: In complex frontend applications, managing asynchronous state using fragmented boolean flags (isLoading, hasError, data) inevitably yields impossible states (e.g. rendering both loading spinner and error alert simultaneously).
sections.initial-approach: Naive approaches often resort to any or unsafe as Type assertions, circumventing TypeScript's safety guarantees entirely.
sections.optimization-thinking:
Model application state with Discriminated Unions:

  • Every state variant possesses a single discriminator property (e.g. status: 'success' | 'error').
  • Custom Type Guards provide foolproof, safe type narrowing.
  • Apply the never type for exhaustive compile-time pattern matching.
sections.code-implementation:
Type-safe asynchronous state management:

type AsyncState =
  | { status: 'idle' }
  | { status: 'loading' }
  | { status: 'success'; data: T }
  | { status: 'error'; error: Error };

function renderState(state: AsyncState) {
  switch (state.status) {
    case 'success': return renderUser(state.data);
    case 'error': return renderError(state.error);
    case 'loading': return ;
    case 'idle': return null;
  }
}
sections.complexity-applications: Eliminated 100% of runtime Cannot read properties of undefined exceptions and elevated engineering velocity through rich IDE IntelliSense autocomplete.

title: System Design Interview Playbook for Senior & Lead: 4-Step Framework and Trade-off Mental Models
summary: Essential guide to mastering large-scale system design interviews: From clarifying ambiguities and back-of-the-envelope calculations to rigorous trade-off evaluations.
author: Huỳnh Nhật Tân

sections.introduction: System design interviews evaluate an engineer's technical depth, structured problem solving, and practical trade-off intuition. This guide distills learnings from evaluating dozens of Senior and Lead candidates.
sections.multi-dimensional-evaluation:
Standard 4-step framework for tackling system design challenges:

  • Step 1: Clarify Scope & Requirements: Delineate functional vs non-functional constraints (QPS, DAU, latency SLA, consistency models).
  • Step 2: Back-of-the-Envelope Estimation: Calculate read/write throughput, 5-year storage capacity, and network egress bandwidth.
  • Step 3: High-Level Architecture: Diagram end-to-end data flows from Client -> CDN / API Gateway -> Microservices -> Cache -> Database.
  • Step 4: Deep Dive & Bottlenecks: Address single points of failure, partition sharding schemes, and CAP theorem consistency boundaries.
sections.case-study-experience: URL Shortener case study: Rather than immediately pitching Redis or Kafka, exceptional candidates first calculate the Read:Write ratio (100:1) to mathematically justify the caching layer.
sections.actionable-recommendations: There are no silver bullets in distributed systems. Always proactively articulate the trade-offs of your chosen architectural decisions.

title: Large-Scale Real-Time Notification System Architecture with WebSockets & Redis Pub/Sub
summary: Designing a distributed WebSocket cluster supporting 100,000+ concurrent connections with Redis Adapter and reliable message replay buffer.
author: Huỳnh Nhật Tân

sections.context-problem: When applications scale to hundreds of thousands of concurrent active users, conventional HTTP polling for notifications severely overloads database servers and consumes excessive network bandwidth. The system demands low-latency real-time event delivery below 200ms.
sections.system-requirements:
• Throughput & Concurrency: Maintain 100,000+ concurrent WebSocket connections across a multi-node cluster.
  • Latency & Reliability: Deliver notifications within 200ms with At-Least-Once guarantees and automated client reconnection.
sections.architecture-design:
Distributed WebSocket architecture utilizing Redis Pub/Sub as the central message bus:

  • WebSocket Gateway: Node.js / Go cluster managing stateful socket connections with clients.
  • Redis Pub/Sub Bus: New notifications are published to user-specific channels and broadcast to the specific cluster node holding the connection.
  • Message Replay Buffer: Retain the last 50 messages on Redis Streams to replay missed alerts upon client reconnection.
sections.trade-offs-analysis:
Comparing pure WebSockets versus Server-Sent Events (SSE):

  • SSE: Simpler, runs over HTTP/2, but only supports unidirectional server-to-client streaming.
  • WebSocket: Full-duplex communication requiring stateful connection management, yet uniquely suited for two-way interactive features (presence, typing indicators, acknowledgments).
sections.lessons-best-practices: Always enforce a 30-second Heartbeat / Ping-Pong cycle to prune dead zombie connections, and configure Nginx Load Balancer with proxy_set_header Upgrade $http_upgrade;.

title: Applying Event Sourcing & CQRS in Stream Processing with Kafka Streams
summary: Guaranteeing immutable financial audit logs and restoring localized State Stores for real-time analytical queries.
author: Huỳnh Nhật Tân

sections.business-data-requirements: In digital banking and payment ledgers, directly updating balances with UPDATE balance = balance + x risks losing critical audit history during dispute reconciliation or concurrency race conditions.
sections.data-modeling:
Event Sourcing models state changes as an append-only stream of immutable facts:

  • Event Log: AccountOpened, MoneyDeposited, and MoneyWithdrawn events are sequenced in Kafka topics partitioned by account_id.
  • Read Model (CQRS): PostgreSQL / Elasticsearch databases hold projections optimized specifically for read-heavy API queries.
sections.pipeline-construction:
Kafka Streams topology architecture:

  • KStream & KTable: Leverage KTable backed by local RocksDB state stores to continuously aggregate balances.
  • Changelog Topic: State Stores continuously synchronize to Kafka Changelog topics for instant disaster recovery upon container failover.
sections.testing-optimization: Stress testing with TopologyTestDriver simulating 50,000 events/sec. Tuned RocksDB block cache allocations and set commit.interval.ms = 100 to minimize disk write amplification.
sections.summary-recommendations: Event Sourcing provides 100% transparent auditability and time-travel debugging capabilities. Recommendation: Implement periodic Snapshotting to avoid prolonged log replay during system warm-up at scale.
